extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, policymakers, and general readers interested in public opinion, propaganda, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and heuristics for recognizing how codes and stereotypes shape perception, judgment, and public opinion, and how to detect their distortions in political and social discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception shaped by stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The way we see things is a combination of what is there and of what we expected to find; our 'constellations of imagery' vibrate to stimuli vaguely similar to aspects of them, so stereotypes strongly determine what we notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mistaking a stranger on a platform by the shape of a hat; an astronomer and a pair of lovers seeing different heavens; a page of Kant producing different trains of thought in different readers. Anti-pattern: treating perception as neutral and assuming disagreements are merely about value rather than about differing perceived facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertness increases discriminations and discounts expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness is a multiplication of the number of aspects we are prepared to discover, plus the habit of discounting our expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: specialists see many highly individual distinctions (chauffeur, epicure, connoisseur). Caveat: limited expertness applies only to certain topics; overconfidence in limited expertness can exaggerate stereotyping and exclude what doesn't fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes lead to retrospective attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When we seek to describe actually successful men and events, we read back into them the qualities presupposed in the stereotypes — the simplified diagrams used for thinking are often 'retail[ed] and popularized' into prevailing mythology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: older economists' simplified model of capitalist/entrepreneur/workman became an 'economic mythology' that people used to explain success; anti-pattern is accepting stereotyped biographies as literal explanations of how success was achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation bias: attention called to supporting facts and diverted from contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a system of stereotypes is well fixed, our attention is called to those facts which support it and diverted from those which contradict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: captains of industry seeing trusts as monuments of success while vanquished competitors see monuments of failure. Detection: look for selective citation of statistics and anecdotes that support opposing stereotyped narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes carry affective loading and pre-judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are loaded with preference, suffused with affection or dislike, attached to fears, lusts, strong wishes, pride, hope — so judgments often precede evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: seeing 'a dewy morn' or 'a dangerous Red' and making moral judgments long before evidence; anti-pattern: assuming moral neutrality of perception. Remedy: deliberately keep prejudice in suspense; cultivate critical habit to recognize opinions as partial experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral codes rest on specific assumptions about facts and human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: At the core of every moral code is a picture of human nature, a map of the universe, and a version of history; the rules of a code apply to situations that match those assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: different codes (personal, family, economic, professional, legal, patriotic, international) may presuppose incompatible views of human nature and history. Example: patriotic code vs commercial code assume different motives for soldiers and contractors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth lacks critical apparatus to separate truth from error
rubrics_metrics.description: A myth may contain much that is true, but it never contains the critical power to separate its truths from its errors; that power comes only by treating opinions as hypotheses subject to evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Even widely held or ancient beliefs should be treated as tentative and tested; anti-pattern: treating myth-derived codes as if they have the same status as evidence-tested science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in assumed facts causes mutual suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone's moral system rests on an accepted version of the facts, denial of either the moral judgment or the version of the facts makes the opponent seem perverse, alien, or dangerous; people rarely recognize that opponents may simply see different facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: To promote tolerance, habituate recognition that opinions are partial and shaped by stereotypes; detection: consider whether disagreement is about facts perceived rather than motives or honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes produce absolutism that censors objections and escalates conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking 'eternal principles' (e.g., historic right, natural boundaries) censors objections, isolates issues from context, stimulates inappropriate strong emotions, and makes accommodation difficult — leading to escalating defenses and fighting rather than discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: territorial claims divided into sectors each justified by a different 'absolute' principle in Ruritanian propaganda. Detection: watch for absolutist language that ignores trade-offs and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection clue — contradictions reveal constructed arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: A rapid succession of contradictory principles or justifications in an argument is a clue that stereotypes are being used to obliterate inconvenient facts; contradiction of this sort often indicates false absolutism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ruritania invoking geographic, historic, cultural, and defensive principles inconsistently for different territories — the contradictions reveal propaganda construction. Use this as a diagnostic when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection clue — inability to take account of space (practical geography)
rubrics_metrics.description: One sign of a stereotype-driven view is failure to account for real spatial constraints (transportation, distance, infrastructure) and treating geometric proximity as sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advocates demanding 'reestablishment of an Eastern Front' ignoring 5,000 miles and broken transport; phantom armies imagined because distance was mentally elided. Check logistics and transportation realities, not just map lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space must be conceived practically (transportation and routes), not geometrically
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical space depends on available transportation, routes, speed, and costs; telling someone 'it's three miles' is misleading unless you specify mode and conditions — the relevant distance is what the actor must traverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: motorist cares about a nine-mile route with ruts, not three miles as the crow flies; boundary lines drawn on maps without surveying produce absurd frontiers (through factories, churches). When assessing claims based on maps, inquire about practical on-the-ground geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection clue — failure to take account of time and appropriate time-conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes often ignore varying time scales; one must distinguish the relevant time-conception (specious present, short-term emergency, long-run consequences) to judge rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: wills and constitutions showing overconfidence about the future; the 'specious present' (~six seconds) vs ideational present for memory. Practical test: ask whether decisions are being made for the next two hours, next decade, or generations, and whether the agent has used the correct time perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness proportional to discriminations affects time perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Vividness (number of discriminations perceived) affects our sense of duration; high discrimination makes time seem long in memory though short in experience, influencing how events are interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from James: creatures perceiving many more events per second would subjectively live much shorter lives; implications for how intense or repetitive experiences shape public memory and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tailored stereotypes in persuasion/propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilled persuaders/diplomats employ a repertory of stereotypes and select the one most likely to resonate with a particular audience or ally, thereby obscuring facts inconvenient to the persuader's aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ruritanian statesmen dividing claims into sectors and invoking different principles (historic right, natural frontier, cultural superiority, defense) to appeal to different audiences. Detection: identify which stereotype is being invoked and for whom; evaluate consistency across sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes produce role-dependent versions of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and societies hold multiple codes (family, business, patriotic), and each code presupposes a version of human nature that may differ greatly; thereby the same person can behave inconsistently across roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a loving father who is a sour boss and a rapacious jingo abroad. Avoid overgeneralization about 'human nature' and examine which code governs a given action when evaluating behavior or policy.
